'''Bertram Claude Brookes''' (7 February 1910 – 10 June 1991) was a [[British Empire|British]] [[statistician]] and [[Information science|information scientist]]. He was best known for his research in [[informetrics]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Shaw |first=Alexandra |date=1990-02-01 |title=B.C. Brookes and the development of information science: a bibliography |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/016555159001600102 |journal=Journal of Information Science |language=EN |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=4 |doi=10.1177/016555159001600102 |issn=0165-5515|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Tague-Suteliffe |first=J. |date=1992 |title=In memoriam B.C. (bertie) brookes, 1910-1991 |url=https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1097-4571(199205)43:4<273::AID-ASI1>3.0.CO;2-A |journal=Journal of the American Society for Information Science (1986-1998) |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=273}}</ref> particularly for reformulating [[Bradford's law|Bradford's Law]] for applications in [[academic library]] management and [[Bibliometrics|bibliometric studies]]. Brookes also made pioneering contributions to the philosophical foundations and methodologies of the emerging field of [[information science]] during the 1970s.

== Life ==
Brookes studied [[physics]] at [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=B. C. Brookes - Biographical Directory of Documentation and Information |url=https://asist.a2hosted.com/index.php/B._C._Brookes |access-date=2025-10-27 |website=asist.a2hosted.com}}</ref> After serving in the [[Royal Air Force]] and the [[Ministry of Supply]] during the [[World War II|Second World War]], he joined [[University College London|University College London (UCL)]] in 1947.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> Until 1968, he was a [[lecturer]] in UCL's Department of Electrical Engineering.

From 1966 until his retirement from [[University College London]] in 1977, he was a professor at the [https://www.ucl.ac.uk/~uczcsuh/slais/aboutslais/aboutslais.html#:~:text=The%20history%20of%20the%20School,Administration%20was%20added%20in%201947. School of Librarianship and Archives], now known as the Department of Information Studies. From 1964 to 1975 Brookes was a member of the editorial board of the ''[[Journal of Documentation]]'', and he has been on the editorial board of the ''[[Journal of Information Science]]'' since 1982.<ref name=":0" /> He subsequently held visiting professorships at the [[University of Western Ontario]] and, from 1984 until his death in 1991, at [[City University London]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> Brookes died on 10  June 1991 at London.<ref name=":4" />

== Research and teaching ==

=== Research on Bradford's law and bibliometrics ===
In 1968, Brookes published his first major work on the application of [[Bradford's law]] in libraries,<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Brookes |first=B.C. |date=1968-04-01 |title=THE DERIVATION AND APPLICATION OF THE BRADFORD‐ZIPF DISTRIBUTION |url=http://www.emerald.com/jd/article/24/4/247-265/206780 |journal=Journal of Documentation |language=en |volume=24 |issue=4 |pages=247–265 |doi=10.1108/eb026457 |issn=0022-0418|url-access=subscription }}</ref> followed by a ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' article in 1969 <ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Brookes |first=B. C. |date=1969 |title=Bradford's Law and the Bibliography of Science |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/224953a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=224 |issue=5223 |pages=953–956 |doi=10.1038/224953a0 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and a series of subsequent publications that spanned his career.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cocks |first=T.M. |last2=Brookes |first2=B.C. |date=1986-02-01 |title=Sichel's unification of bibliometric frequency distributions |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/016555158601200108 |journal=Journal of Information Science |language=EN |volume=12 |issue=1-2 |pages=45–51 |doi=10.1177/016555158601200108 |issn=0165-5515|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brookes |first=B.C. |date=1988-08-01 |title=Sichel's inverse Gaussian-Poisson distribution: recent advances |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/016555158801400405 |journal=Journal of Information Science |language=EN |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=233–236 |doi=10.1177/016555158801400405 |issn=0165-5515|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Hood |first=William W. |last2=Wilson |first2=Concepción S. |date=2001-10-01 |title=The Literature of Bibliometrics, Scientometrics, and Informetrics |url=https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1017919924342 |journal=Scientometrics |language=en |volume=52 |issue=2 |pages=291–314 |doi=10.1023/A:1017919924342 |issn=1588-2861|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Brookes's research on Bradford's law was not only a highlight of his career<ref name=":0" /> but also laid the foundation for a systematic study of bibliometric distributions, which continues to shape the field of [[bibliometrics]] today.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Oluić-Vuković |first=Vesna |date=1997 |title=Bradford's distribution: From the classical bibliometric "law" to the more general stochastic models |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/%28SICI%291097-4571%28199709%2948%3A9%3C833%3A%3AAID-ASI7%3E3.0.CO%3B2-S |journal=Journal of the American Society for Information Science |language=en |volume=48 |issue=9 |pages=833–842 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1097-4571(199709)48:9<833::AID-ASI7>3.0.CO;2-S |issn=1097-4571|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Bradford's law, first proposed by British mathematician and librarian [[Samuel C. Bradford]] in 1934,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brookes |first=B.C. |date=1985-04-01 |title="Sources of information on specific subjects" by S.C. Bradford |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/016555158501000406 |journal=Journal of Information Science |language=EN |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=173–175 |doi=10.1177/016555158501000406 |issn=0165-5515|url-access=subscription }}</ref> describes how scholarly articles on a given subject are distributed across journals. It observes that a small core of journals produces the majority of significant papers on a topic, while a much larger number of journals publish only a few relevant articles each. When Brookes began his research, the application of [[Bradford's law]] in library settings was limited. The calculations then required researchers to identify a large number of peripheral papers and perform complex computations—tasks that were time-consuming and discouraged practical use. As a result, the law had remained, in Brookes's words, a mere statistical curiosity.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Brookes |first=B.C. |date=1985 |title="Sources of information on specific subjects" by S.C. Bradford |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/016555158501000406 |journal=Journal of Information Science |language=en |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=173–175 |doi=10.1177/016555158501000406 |issn=0165-5515|url-access=subscription }}</ref><sup>p.&nbsp;175</sup>

Brookes proposed that, with the emerging use of computer-based search systems, Bradford's law could be transformed into a practical tool for libraries.<ref name=":7" /> By focusing on the most productive journals, librarians could efficiently generate subject bibliographies and estimate the scope of literature within a given field. He also introduced a modified form of the Bradford distribution that combined its principles with those of the [[Zipf's law|Zipf distribution]],<ref name=":1" /> developed by linguist [[George Kingsley Zipf]] in the 1930s and 1940s. Zipf's distribution describes an inverse relationship between the frequency and rank of an item in naturally occurring datasets, such as word frequencies in language. By linking these two statistical models, Brookes streamlined the process of literature estimation and bibliographic generation, making [[Bradford's law|Bradford's Law]] a practical instrument for [[information retrieval]] and [[library management]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" />

=== The fundamental equation ===
Brookes is often associated with the cognitive turn in information science through his "fundamental equation", sometimes also known as "foundational equation", which models information as a change in a person’s knowledge structure: K[S] + ΔI = K[S + ΔS]. <ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Cole |first=Charles |date=1997-11-01 |title=Calculating the information content of an information process for a domain expert using Shannon's mathematical theory of communication: A preliminary analysis |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306457397000381 |journal=Information Processing & Management |volume=33 |issue=6 |pages=715–726 |doi=10.1016/S0306-4573(97)00038-1 |issn=0306-4573|url-access=subscription }}</ref>In this equation, information ( ΔI ) is defined as capable of modifying knowledge structure, which views information not only as something that is added to the mind, but also as a state of informativeness, the meaning of which varies by person and situation. <ref name=":8" />

=== Development of library and information science pedagogy ===
Although Brookes's most frequently cited and widely remembered works concern his research on [[bibliometrics]] and the reformulation of [[Bradford's law]],<ref name=":0" /> his teaching was also regarded as one of the pioneering efforts in the pedagogy of [[library and information science]]. Brookes's work as an educator, shaping the discipline's intellectual foundations and classroom practices during its formative decades between the 1950s and 1970s, was equally influential and remains what many of his students remember most vividly.<ref name=":4" /> After his appointment in 1947 as [[lecturer]] at [[University College London|University College London (UCL)]], Brookes taught courses in [[statistics]] for [[engineering]]<ref name=":0" /> and co-authored the textbook ''Introduction to Statistical Method'' with W. F. L. Dick,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Brookes |first=B. C. |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/006242340 |title=Introduction to statistical method |last2=Dick |first2=William Francis Lawson |date=1953 |publisher=Heinemann on label: distributed by W.S. Heinmann, New York |location=London}}</ref> with various emended editions published between the 1950s and 1970s.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Campbell |first=R. C. |date=1970 |title=Introduction to Statistical Method. By B. C. Brookes and W. F. L. Dick. Second Edition. Part 1, Pp. xii, 142; Part 2, Pp. 190. 18s. 1969 (Heinemann.) |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S002555720012577X/type/journal_article |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |language=en |volume=54 |issue=389 |pages=323–323 |doi=10.2307/3613839 |issn=0025-5572|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The book was widely adopted in U.K. schools<ref name=":6" />  and was praised as a pioneering work in statistical education.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Armitage |first=P. |date=1952 |title=Review of Introduction to Statistical Method. |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2981115 |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series A (General) |volume=115 |issue=1 |pages=139–139 |doi=10.2307/2981115 |issn=0035-9238|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Brookes was also among the earliest pioneers to incorporate statistical methods into the training of library and information management. As early as 1967, he taught a course introducing performance measurement and quantitative evaluation techniques for library management,<ref name=":0" /> and he also published extensively on the pedagogy of library and information science training.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wishart |first=John |date=1953 |title=Review of Notes on the Teaching of Statistics in Schools. |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2981064 |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series A (General) |volume=116 |issue=2 |pages=203–204 |doi=10.2307/2981064 |issn=0035-9238|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Conway |first=Freda |date=1986 |title=Statistics in Schools |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2981885 |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series A (General) |volume=149 |issue=1 |pages=60–64 |doi=10.2307/2981885 |issn=0035-9238|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Recognition and legacy ==
In 1989, Brookes received the [[Derek J. de Solla Price|Derek John de Solla Price]] Memorial Award,<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=Derek de Solla Price Memorial Medal |url=https://www.issi-society.org/awards/derek-de-solla-price-memorial-medal/ |access-date=2025-10-27 |website=International Society for Scientometrics and Informetrics |language=en}}</ref> presented jointly to him and Czechoslovak information scientist [[:de:Jan Vlachý|Jan Vlachý]]. The international award, established in 1984 in honor of information scientist [[Derek J. de Solla Price]], recognizes outstanding contributions to the field of scientometrics and information science.<ref name=":12" />

Brookes's work has been read internationally and translated into several languages.<ref name=":0" /> Throughout his career, he traveled widely, teaching and presenting papers at conferences and seminars across Europe and North America. At both [[City St George's, University of London|City University of London]] and [[University College London]], he taught students from around the world and became known for his rigorous yet inspiring teaching style and communication skills.<ref name=":0" /> He was highly regarded by colleagues and students alike, not only as a pioneering researcher, but also as a generous mentor and peer.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" />
